newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli soldier shoots up Hebron market.
newsitem.headline: Israeli soldier shoots up Hebron market.

text.p: An Israeli soldier sprayed rifle fire into a Hebron market on Wednesday wounding seven Arabs in what he called an attempt to keep the city from being handed over to Palestinian rule.

The off-duty soldier, who lives in a Jewish settlement near Jerusalem, emptied the clip of his M-16 automatic rifle into the crowded open-air market before other soldiers overpowered him, witnesses said.
"Even after soldiers had wrestled him to the ground he tried to put a second magazine into his gun," said Reuters cameraman Mazen Dana.

Noam Friedman, wearing the skullcap and tassled undershirt of a religious Jew, smirked and shook his fist on leaving a police station after the attack which was condemned by U.S. President Bill Clinton and Israeli leaders.
His defiance brought to mind another right-wing, religious Israeli, Yigal Amir, who murdered prime minister Yitzhak Rabin.
"Abraham bought the Cave of the Patriarchs for 400 shekels of silver and nobody will give it back," Friedman told reporters, referring to the biblical Abraham.

The Cave, where 29 Moslems were massacred by a settler three years ago, is holy to Jews and Moslems. It is to remain under Israeli control along with all Jewish holy places after Israel withdraws from 80 percent of Hebron.

Friedman, 19, from Maale Adumim settlement near Jerusalem, fired for nearly 10 seconds into the vegetable market on Martyrs Street wounding men, women and a youth, witnesses and doctors said. Two of the injured were in critical condition.

Palestinians hurled themselves to the ground shouting "massacre" when the bullets started flying. Soldiers and police, thinking they were under attack, ran to the market from the Avraham Avinu settlement firing, witnesses said. One Palestinian man was apparently hit by them.
The army poured troops into the city and put armoured personnel carriers on surrounding hills to prevent reprisals. It also imposed a brief curfew.

Youths burned tyres and clashed with soldiers briefly after the shooting but the streets quickly emptied. Soldiers beat back a crowd that gathered at the market after the shooting, the worst in the city since U.S.-born settler Baruch Goldstein massacred 29 Moslems in 1994.
The shooting underscored the fragility of the U.S.-sponsored Middle East peace process and the feeling of betrayal of right-wing Jews opposed to returning captured land to Arabs.
The United States deplored the shooting and vowed to continue mediating a settlement on the long-delayed Israeli redeployment from 80 percent of Hebron.

"We in the United States condemn this act in the strongest possible terms," U.S. Middle East peace envoy Dennis Ross told reporters in Gaza after meeting Palestinian President Yasser Arafat. Asked if talks would continue, Ross said: "Yes".
Ross met earlier with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu who also condemned the attack.

Ross is trying to arrange an Arafat-Netanyahu summit to close the Hebron deal. PLO officials said Palestinian negotiator Mahmoud Abbas and Israeli Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai would meet later in the day in an effort to keep talks on track.
"I want to say again in a sharp way that no crime and no violent act will stand in the way of our completing the work," Netanyahu told reporters in Jerusalem.
The gunman told investigators he wanted to sabotage the handover, Israel's central area commander Major-General Uzi Dayan said.
"Bibi (Netanyahu) remains alone, without Jews behind him," Friedman said, remarks that again echoed Amir, who killed Rabin 14 months ago to halt a land-for-peace deal with Arafat.
Hebron's Palestinian political leaders issued a statement after the shooting saying there could be no peace while the 400 settlers remained among the 100,000 Palestinians.
"The only solution for Hebron is to evacuate these fanatics," the statement said.
Hebron has been a powderkeg since the Goldstein massacre in the al-Ibrahimi mosque at the Cave of the Patriarchs.

"It happened right in front of me," said vegetable seller Walid Kafisheh, 46, on Wednesday. "I tried to stop him but the soldiers got to him first. Then soldiers and police came from everywhere shooting," he told Reuters.
Israeli lieutenant Avi Buskila grabbed the soldier.

"He entered the area at the square and began shooting into the vegetable market. I stood at my post and heard the shots. Within 10 seconds I pinned him to the ground and took his gun," he told Reuters.
Jewish settlers in the town had said they were praying for a miracle to prevent Israeli troops from pulling back and warned of impending bloodshed.
Jewish settlers, who number 130,000 in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, helped Netanyahu sweep to power in elections last May on a promise to be tough with the Palestinians.

But Netanyahu has come under pressure from Washington, Israel's closest ally, to honour peace deals and withdraw from Hebron, the last of seven West Bank towns due for self-rule under the first stage of the 1993 Oslo peace accord.
